transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's kind of hard to pin down, to be honest. I mean, I'm 63 now, and you expect to slow down a bit, right? But this... mostly I came in because I’m tired in a way that just doesn’t make any sense to me. I mean, I'm sleeping fine. I get my seven, eight hours a night. I get up, I go to work—I manage an IT department, so it's busy, there's always a server down or some software update causing a headache, but I can still keep up with all of it. It's not like I'm falling asleep at my desk or anything like that. But despite all that, despite getting enough sleep and pushing through the day, I still feel like I’m running on a low battery before the day even gets going. You know that feeling when your phone is at 15% right when you take it off the charger in the morning? That's me. I wake up, and I'm already exhausted. And it just lingers. It's this heavy, dull sort of tiredness that just sits there, right behind my eyes, all day long, no matter how much coffee I drink or how well I slept the night before. It's just... it's frustrating, really.
Have you noticed that you’re not enjoying things as much as you used to, or that you’ve lost interest in activities you once found pleasurable?

Well, yes, actually. Now that you mention it, that's... that's a big part of it, too. It's not just the tiredness, though they sort of bleed into each other, don't they? But yes, for a long time now—I mean, years, probably, if I really stop and think about it—there's just been this... this gray, flat feeling. Most days, anyway. It's like the volume has been turned down on everything good. 

Take my fishing, for example. I used to love getting out on the lake early Saturday morning, just me and the quiet. I’d spend all week looking forward to it. But lately... well, for a good while now, I drag myself out of bed, load up the gear, and I'm out there on the water, and I just feel... nothing. It's the same with my garden. I used to take real pride in my tomatoes. I’d be out there checking the soil, pruning the leaves, waiting for that first red one to come in. Now, I go out there and water them, but it just feels like another chore. Like mowing the lawn or taking out the trash. Even when Mary—my wife—drags me to one of those church concerts we used to enjoy so much, I sit there in the pew, listening to the choir, and I'm just waiting for it to be over so I can go home. It's like everything I used to look forward to is just an item on a checklist now. I do them because I'm supposed to, or because it's what I've always done, but the joy... the actual enjoyment of it... it's just not there anymore. It's just flat. Everything is just flat.
Would you say that your mood has been consistently low or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, and not just occasionally feeling down or tired?

Well, yes, exactly. That's... that's really hitting the nail on the head, doctor. It's not just a passing thing, you know? It's not like I had a bad day at work because the servers crashed and I came home grumpy. It's... it's this constant, lingering thing. Like I was saying before about the fishing and the tomatoes and the concerts with Mary... it's all part of this same, overarching feeling. Or lack of feeling, really. 

It's just this gray, flat sensation that sits with me most of the day, pretty much every single day. I wake up with it, I take it to work with me, I bring it home. It's like a fog that just won't lift. And it's been going on for such a long time now. I can't even pinpoint exactly when it started, it just sort of crept in and unpacked its bags and decided to stay. So, yes, it's definitely not just occasionally feeling a bit blue or tired. It's a consistent, heavy sort of flatness where everything just feels like a chore, like checking boxes on a list, instead of actually living and enjoying my life. It's just... always there.
Doctor: Can you recall if there was ever a period of at least two weeks when your mood was down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, and you lost interest or pleasure in most activities?

Well, I mean... a period of two weeks? Honestly, doctor, it's... it's hard to chop it up into two-week blocks like that. It's not like I mark it on the calendar, you know? "Started feeling bad on the 14th, felt a bit better by the 28th." It's just... it's more of a blur than that. 

Like I said, this gray feeling, this flatness where the fishing and the gardening just feel like chores... it's been going on for years. It's not like it comes and goes in sharp little spikes. It's just a constant hum in the background. I mean, sure, there are days that are slightly better or slightly worse. Like, maybe a Tuesday is a little heavier because we had a massive network outage at work and I had to stay late, and then Wednesday I'm just drained. But then Thursday rolls around and it's back to the usual flat, gray fog. 

So, a specific two-week period where it was intensely bad, where I lost interest in *everything*... I don't know. It's just been a steady drip, drip, drip of losing interest over a long time. It didn't just crash down on me all at once for a fortnight and then vanish. It's just... it's just my life now, really. It's always there, stretching out behind me for longer than I can really put a date on. So, I can't really single out a specific two weeks, no. It's just one long stretch of this... this same feeling.
Would you say that this low, flat mood you’ve been experiencing has been present most of the day, more days than not, for at least the past two years?

Well, yes. Yes, I can actually put a bit of a timeline on that, now that you frame it that way. Two years... yes, it’s been longer than that, actually. It really all started—this whole gray, flat stretch—when they pulled me back into full operational leadership at the company. That was... let's see, it would have been about two years and four months ago, exactly. 

You see, I had stepped back a bit, taken on more of an advisory role with the IT department, trying to slow down, maybe enjoy things a bit more. But then we had this massive restructuring, and the new director left suddenly, and well, they needed someone who knew the legacy systems inside and out. So, boom, right back into the thick of it. Managing the whole information systems team again, dealing with all the fires, the server migrations, the personnel issues. And almost from the moment I moved back into that corner office, this... this fog just settled in. 

I remember thinking it was just the stress of the transition, you know? Adjusting to the long hours again, the constant emails. I told Mary, "Just give it a few months, once the new software rollout is done, things will get back to normal." But the rollout finished, and then it was the quarterly audits, and then it was the budget cuts... and the feeling just never lifted. It just stayed. Two years and four months of waking up, dragging myself in, putting out fires all day, and coming home too drained to even look at my fishing gear or care about the garden. So, yes, more days than not, most of the day... it’s been a constant companion since that promotion—if you can call it that—two years and four months ago. It hasn't let up since.
Have you noticed a significant loss of energy or increased fatigue, even when you're not doing anything particularly strenuous?

Well, yes, actually. That's... that's really the main reason I finally decided to come in and see someone. The fatigue. It's just... it's profound, doctor. And it doesn't make any logical sense, which is what's so frustrating about it. I mean, I'm an IT manager, my whole career is built on logic and troubleshooting, right? If a server is running slow, you check the memory, you check the CPU usage, you find the bottleneck. But with me... I just can't find the bottleneck. 

I'm tired in this deep, heavy way that just defies explanation. I mean, I'm sleeping. I go to bed at a reasonable hour, I'm not tossing and turning all night, I'm getting my seven or eight hours. And I'm still keeping up at work, mostly because I have to. I push through the meetings, I sign off on the budgets, I handle the escalations. I'm not doing physical labor, I'm not out there digging ditches or hauling equipment around. I sit at a desk, I look at screens, I talk to people. It's not strenuous in a physical sense at all. 

But despite all that, despite the sleep and the lack of physical exertion, I still feel like I'm just... running on a low battery. And it's not just at the end of the day, either. That's the kicker. It's before the day even really gets going. I'll wake up, have my coffee, and as I'm pulling out of the driveway to head to the office, I already feel this bone-deep exhaustion. It's like my internal power supply is just faulty. I'm at 20% before I even log into my workstation. I try to explain it to Mary, and she says maybe I need vitamins or maybe I'm fighting off a bug, but it's been going on for so long. It's just this constant, heavy tiredness that sits on top of everything else, making even the simplest things—like just getting through a Tuesday morning staff meeting—feel like I'm wading through wet cement. So, yes, the loss of energy is... it's very significant. It's honestly the most baffling part of all this.
Have you experienced any other symptoms along with this fatigue and low mood, such as changes in your appetite, weight, concentration, or thoughts about death or dying?

Thoughts about dying? Oh, no, no, nothing like that, doctor. Goodness, no. I'm just tired, not giving up. And my concentration... well, I manage to keep the department running, like I said. But the appetite... yes, that's actually something Mary was just bringing up the other day. It’s funny you ask about that, because it’s been off more days than not lately. 

I used to be a real stickler for my lunch break, you know? 12:30 PM sharp, I’d step away from the monitors, maybe go down to the deli on the corner or the building cafeteria, get a turkey club, just try to clear my head for half an hour. But lately, with this whole gray fog and the tiredness I was telling you about... I just sit there. I'll be looking at a server migration schedule or a vendor contract, and suddenly I look at the clock and it's 3:00 PM and I haven't eaten a thing. I just work right through lunch without even noticing I'm hungry. My stomach doesn't rumble, I don't get that mid-day craving... nothing. It's like the signal just isn't getting through.

And then, when I finally get home, Mary will have cooked—she makes these wonderful dinners, always has, a nice roast or chicken, she's a fantastic cook—and I just sit there picking at it. I push the food around my plate, take a couple of bites, and I'm just... done. I'm not full, really, just totally disinterested. I just don't have the drive to eat. 

And because of all this, I've actually dropped some weight. I wasn't even keeping track, to be honest with you, but Mary pointed it out last weekend when we were getting ready to head out. She said my slacks were looking terribly baggy. And she’s right, my pants are definitely looser. I’m having to pull my belt a whole notch tighter just to keep them from sliding down. And I’m certainly not trying to lose weight—at my age, you don't really want to be fluctuating too much, and I've never been one for diets anyway. But it's just happening on its own because I just can't seem to muster up the interest in a meal anymore.
Have you found yourself feeling guilty or blaming yourself for things more than usual, or feeling like you’re not living up to your own or others’ expectations?

Guilty? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean... I don't really sit around beating myself up over things. Like I was saying about the IT department, I still get the job done. I might be running on a low battery, but I'm still keeping the servers online, I'm still managing the team, and I'm still hitting all our quarterly metrics. If anything, the higher-ups are probably thrilled with how the legacy systems are holding up since I took the reins back. So I certainly don't feel like I'm failing them. I know I'm putting in the hours and doing exactly what they pay me to do, even if it feels like wading through wet cement to get it done. 

And at home with Mary... well, bless her heart, she doesn't put any pressure on me, so I don't feel like I'm letting her down, either. We've been married a long time, over thirty years now, and she knows my work ethic inside and out. She knows that if I'm just sitting in my armchair on a Saturday afternoon instead of out tinkering with my fishing gear or weeding the tomato beds, it's not because I'm lazy or trying to shirk my chores around the house. She sees how drained I am. 

So, no, I don't have this... this internal voice telling me I'm a failure or that I'm not living up to expectations. It's really more of a frustration, if I'm being honest. A logical frustration. It’s like having a machine on the network that isn't operating at peak efficiency, but it's still passing all the basic diagnostic tests, you know? You don't blame the machine, you don't get mad at it, you just want to figure out why the output is suddenly so low. That’s how I view myself right now. I know my own worth, I know my track record. I'm just tired. So, no, guilt really isn't a factor here at all.
Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly than usual, or feeling restless and unable to sit still?

Moving slowly? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I'm exhausted, like I was telling you, but when I actually need to get up and walk down the hall to the server room or head out to the car, my legs work just fine. I walk at my normal pace. I'm not shuffling along or moving in slow motion like some wind-up toy winding down. The physical mechanics are all there, it's just the battery that's low, if we're keeping with that analogy. 

And as for being restless or unable to sit still? Oh, definitely not. If anything, sitting still is exactly what I prefer to do right now. I have this really great ergonomic chair at the office—an Aeron chair, you know the ones with the gray mesh backing? We managed to get them for the whole IT department a few years back when we had a little surplus in the Q4 equipment budget, and honestly, it's a lifesaver for the lumbar spine. I can sit in that thing for hours. I don't get the urge to pace around or tap my feet or anything like that. 

You see some of these younger guys, the junior developers on my team, and they've got the standing desks, or they're pacing the floor with their wireless headsets during conference calls, just constantly fidgeting and bouncing off the walls. I've never been much like that anyway, but especially not lately. Once I sit down at my workstation, I'm pretty much planted there. And at home, it's the same story with my armchair in the den. So, no, the physical movement itself hasn't really changed. I'm not agitated and I'm not physically slowed down. It's really just that internal, heavy sense of fatigue I mentioned before.
Have you ever had a period in the past when you experienced a low mood and loss of interest in activities for at least two weeks, before the current episode began two years ago?

Before these last two years? No, no, never anything like this. I mean, I’ve always been a pretty steady guy, mood-wise. Even back when things were incredibly stressful at work... like, oh, I don't know, during the big data center migration we did back in 2015, or even way back during the Y2K scare. You remember that, right? Goodness, everyone in the industry thought the sky was falling. We were working eighty-hour weeks, sleeping under our desks, eating cold pizza out of the breakroom fridge... but even then, I never felt *low*, you know? I was stressed, sure, and exhausted from the sheer hours, but not this... this gray fog I've been in lately. 

Back then, and really for my whole life up until a couple of years ago, I always bounced right back. I still looked forward to getting home to Mary. I still couldn't wait for Saturday morning so I could get out to the lake with my fishing gear or get my hands dirty in the tomato beds. I always had my projects and my interests. I was always the guy who had his engine running at a nice, steady hum. 

So, no, I've never had a two-week stretch—or even a one-week stretch, really—where I just lost interest in things or felt down in the dumps like this. It really just started creeping up on me about two years ago, almost like a slow leak in a tire. Before that, my track record was solid. I was always engaged, always ready to tackle the day. This whole business of just... existing... it's strictly a recent development for me.
Have you found yourself feeling worse about who you are, or feeling like you're not as good as you used to be at things, even if you can't quite put your finger on why?

Feeling worse about myself? Or feeling like I'm not as good as I used to be? Well... no, I wouldn't frame it quite like that. I mean, it goes back to what I was saying earlier about the IT department and how I view myself. I know my own worth. I know exactly what I'm capable of. 

Take my coding skills, for example. I'm an old-school guy, right? I learned on languages that most of these kids straight out of college have only ever read about in their history of computing courses. I know the legacy systems we run at the office inside and out because I helped build the architecture for them twenty-something years ago. If there's a critical error in one of the old databases, I know exactly which line of code to look at, while the junior devs are still trying to figure out how to even access the directory. My expertise hasn't diminished one bit. My brain still holds all that knowledge. I haven't lost my touch or my intelligence.

So I don't sit there thinking, "Oh, I'm a terrible manager," or "I'm not good at my job anymore." I know I'm good at it. I know I'm a good husband to Mary, too. I've always been a steady provider, a loyal partner. We've built a wonderful life together in our home—the one we bought back in '98, over in the Oak Creek subdivision. It's a great house, solid foundation, nice big yard for my tomatoes. I've maintained that house beautifully over the years. 

It's just... it's just the energy, you know? It's the fatigue. It's not a question of my *ability* or my *worth*, it's a question of my *capacity* right now. I don't feel bad about *who* I am. I'm the same guy I've always been. I'm just a version of that guy who feels like he's trying to run a marathon in waist-deep water. It's frustrating, absolutely, because I know what I *could* be doing if I just had the energy I used to have, but I don't internalize it as a flaw in my character or a loss of my skills. I know the engine is still perfectly fine, it's just... well, it's just not getting any gas. So, no, I don't really have those kinds of negative thoughts about myself as a person.

Would you say that your current low mood and loss of interest have reached the point of being a major depressive episode, where you've had several other symptoms nearly every day for at least two weeks, such as feeling down, losing pleasure, changes in appetite, trouble sleeping or sleeping too much, feeling tired, feeling worthless, or having trouble concentrating?

A major episode? With all those things hitting me at once? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, if we're talking about a complete system crash where everything just shuts down and I can't function... no, it hasn't been like that. 

Like I was just saying, I certainly don't feel worthless. And as for the other things you mentioned... well, my appetite hasn't changed a bit. Mary would be the first to tell you if it had. She makes this incredible pot roast on Sundays—she’s been making it the exact same way for probably thirty years now, with the little pearl onions and the carrots—and I still clear my plate every time. And during the week, I still pack my lunch, usually just a turkey sandwich on rye and an apple, and I eat it at my desk while I'm reviewing the morning logs. So food is fine. 

And sleep... well, I sleep alright. I mean, sure, I might doze off in my armchair in the den while we're watching the evening news, but I'm not lying awake all night staring at the ceiling, and I'm certainly not sleeping the days away. I still set my alarm for 6:00 AM sharp every single morning, just like I have since I started at the company, and I get up and take a shower and head out the door. 

So, no, I haven't had any two-week stretch where a whole bunch of those things just piled up on me like a ton of bricks. It’s never been a sudden, severe dip. If you want to put it in IT terms, it's not a total server failure or a blue screen of death. It's really just... it's just this constant, low-level drain. Like a background process that's eating up just enough memory to make the whole system run a little sluggish, but not enough to actually crash the computer. It’s just been this same, flat, gray feeling and that heavy exhaustion stretching on for two solid years now, day in and day out. It never gets drastically worse, but it never really gets better, either. It’s just... there. Always there. But no, not a major episode with all those other problems.
Have you had trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or sleeping too much, even though you feel tired?

Well, like I was saying just a minute ago about my routine, getting to sleep isn't really the issue. I usually fall asleep all right. By the time ten o'clock rolls around, I'm usually pretty beat, so I hit the pillow and I'm out. But... staying asleep, I suppose that's where the gears get a little stuck. 

It’s been happening a lot where I’ll just pop awake, almost like clockwork, right around four in the morning. And it’s not a peaceful waking up, either. It’s like someone flips a switch and my brain is instantly online, already sorting through server issues or stressing over these new compliance deadlines the executives keep handing down to my department. You know how it is with data security these days—it's a never-ending battle to keep the legacy systems up to code, and the audits are just ruthless. So I'll be lying there in the dark, listening to Mary breathe, and my head is just buzzing with patch schedules and security protocols. 

Once that starts, I can't shut it down. I don't want to wake Mary, so I just lie there until the alarm finally goes off at six. So even though I was technically in bed for a solid eight hours, it feels like the night didn’t really count. It’s like putting a computer in sleep mode but the internal fan is still running on high the whole time, just burning up energy. By the time I actually get up to take my shower, I feel like I've already worked half a shift.
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to think clearly, concentrate, or make decisions?

Think clearly? No, no, I wouldn't say that. My mind is still as sharp as a tack. I mean, I think I touched on this a bit earlier when we were talking about my skills, but my concentration is... well, it's perfectly fine. 

Just to give you a concrete example, just last Thursday—no, wait, it was Wednesday, because Mary had her neighborhood watch meeting that evening—we had this massive integration hiccup at the office. The junior developers were trying to sync up this new cloud-based front end with our old SQL databases, and of course, they completely botched the data mapping. It was a mess. I sat at my desk for... gosh, it must have been four or five hours straight, just staring at my dual monitors, tracing the data flows line by line, cross-referencing the old schema. I didn't even get up to get a cup of coffee or use the restroom. You don't do that if you can't concentrate, you know? I was completely dialed in, focused entirely on the code. 

And as for making decisions... well, I'm still the guy everyone comes to when the rubber meets the road. Just yesterday morning, the VP of Operations was waffling on whether we should push a critical security patch during business hours or wait for the weekend maintenance window. He was going back and forth, pacing around my office, holding up the whole department because he was afraid of a temporary outage. I just looked at the risk assessment, saw that the vulnerability was way too high to leave exposed for another three days, and I made the call. Boom. Done. I told him we're pushing the patch at 2:00 PM, I managed the localized server reboots myself, and we were totally secure by 3:30. 

So, no, my decision-making is as solid as it was twenty years ago. The hardware up here in my head—the processor, if you will—is running at optimal speed. It's just that power supply issue I keep coming back to. The physical exhaustion. But the actual thinking? The logic and the focus? No problems there whatsoever. I can still out-think anyone in my department on any given day.
Have you noticed that you’ve been moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or that you’ve been unusually restless or unable to sit still, nearly every day?

Moving slowly or... being restless? No, I wouldn't say so. Not at all, really. 

I mean, I'm sixty-three, so I'm not exactly running the hundred-meter dash like I did back in my high school track days, but I get around the office at the exact same pace I always have. If there's a physical hardware issue down in the server room on the second floor, I'm down the stairs and in the racks just as quick as anyone else. And as for speaking slowly... well, you're listening to me right now. I think I keep a pretty standard cadence. If anything, when I'm explaining a complex network topology to the new hires, I actually have to consciously slow myself down, because they just don't grasp the legacy architecture we're running and I end up losing them if I talk at my normal speed. 

And as for being restless, or not being able to sit still... well, I think I just mentioned a minute ago how I sat at my desk for four or five hours straight working on that SQL database issue without even getting up for coffee. You absolutely cannot do that if you're fidgeting or bouncing your leg or needing to pace the halls. I see some of these young guys, these new junior developers, they come in with their giant energy drinks, and they're tapping their pens, shaking their knees under the desk, constantly getting up to pace around or play ping-pong in the breakroom... I honestly don't know how they get a single line of clean code written with all that nervous energy. 

But me? No, I plant myself in my desk chair—Mary actually bought me this fantastic Herman Miller chair for our anniversary a few years back because the standard issue office chairs were doing a number on my lower back, and let me tell you, it was the best investment we ever made—and I just sit there and work. I don't pace, I don't fidget. I just sit and process the data. So, no, none of that physical slowing down or jittery stuff. I'm physically steady. It's really just that battery drain I keep coming back to.
Would you say that your current low mood and loss of interest in activities have been present for most of the day, more days than not, for the past two years without a significant break?

Well, let me think about that timeframe. Two years... Actually, if I’m being completely precise—and you know how I am with tracking the details—it’s been a bit longer than that. I’d put it right at about two years and four months. 

I know that specifically because, well, that’s exactly when they pulled me back into full operational leadership at the company. See, before that, I had sort of transitioned into more of an advisory role. A senior systems architect position where I was mostly just consulting on the big-picture infrastructure, you know, handing off the day-to-day firefighting to the younger guys so I could coast a bit toward retirement. Mary and I were even looking at buying an RV, mapping out some national parks we wanted to see. 

But then, of course, our director of IT operations decides to jump ship to some fintech startup out in Silicon Valley, and he leaves us completely high and dry right in the middle of a massive, multi-phase server migration. It was total chaos. The executives were panicking. So, management comes to me, practically begging, saying they need someone with institutional knowledge to steer the ship, and before I know it, I’m back in the trenches. Full operational leadership, managing a team of thirty people, dealing with the daily grind all over again. 

And ever since that happened—which, like I said, was exactly two years and four months ago—it’s just been this constant, low-grade... drag. Every single day. Most of the day, really. I wake up with it, like I mentioned with those early morning wake-ups at four AM, and I just carry it with me through the whole shift, and then I drag it back home with me. There really hasn't been a break from it. Not a real one, anyway. Even when Mary and I took a long weekend up to the lake cabin last fall, which was supposed to be a total disconnect, no laptops allowed, I was still just sitting out on the porch feeling completely flat. Just drained of any actual enthusiasm for being there, or for doing much of anything, really. 

So, yes, to answer your question, it’s been more days than not, pretty much all day, without any real interruption, ever since I got pulled back into that role two years and four months ago.

Well, like I was saying just a minute ago about my routine, getting to sleep isn't really the issue. I usually fall asleep all right. By the time ten o'clock rolls around, I'm usually pretty beat, so I hit the pillow and I'm out. But... staying asleep, I suppose that's where the gears get a little stuck. 

It’s been happening a lot where I’ll just pop awake, almost like clockwork, right around four in the morning. And it’s not a peaceful waking up, either. It’s like someone flips a switch and my brain is instantly online, already sorting through server issues or stressing over these new compliance deadlines the executives keep handing down to my department. You know how it is with data security these days—it's a never-ending battle to keep the legacy systems up to code, and the audits are just ruthless. So I'll be lying there in the dark, listening to Mary breathe, and my head is just buzzing with patch schedules and security protocols. 

Once that starts, I can't shut it down. I don't want to wake Mary, so I just lie there until the alarm finally goes off at six. So even though I was technically in bed for a solid eight hours, it feels like the night didn’t really count. It’s like putting a computer in sleep mode but the internal fan is still running on high the whole time, just burning up energy. By the time I actually get up to take my shower, I feel like I've already worked half a shift.

The duration of symptoms exceeds two years, consistent with persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia). No new information has emerged to rule out F33.1 or F33.9.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness, nearly every day.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your ability to think clearly, concentrate, or make decisions?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in concentration, clear thinking, or decision-making, which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Think clearly? No, no, I wouldn't say that. My mind is still as sharp as a tack. I mean, I think I touched on this a bit earlier when we were talking about my skills, but my concentration is... well, it's perfectly fine. 

Just to give you a concrete example, just last Thursday—no, wait, it was Wednesday, because Mary had her neighborhood watch meeting that evening—we had this massive integration hiccup at the office. The junior developers were trying to sync up this new cloud-based front end with our old SQL databases, and of course, they completely botched the data mapping. It was a mess. I sat at my desk for... gosh, it must have been four or five hours straight, just staring at my dual monitors, tracing the data flows line by line, cross-referencing the old schema. I didn't even get up to get a cup of coffee or use the restroom. You don't do that if you can't concentrate, you know? I was completely dialed in, focused entirely on the code. 

And as for making decisions... well, I'm still the guy everyone comes to when the rubber meets the road. Just yesterday morning, the VP of Operations was waffling on whether we should push a critical security patch during business hours or wait for the weekend maintenance window. He was going back and forth, pacing around my office, holding up the whole department because he was afraid of a temporary outage. I just looked at the risk assessment, saw that the vulnerability was way too high to leave exposed for another three days, and I made the call. Boom. Done. I told him we're pushing the patch at 2:00 PM, I managed the localized server reboots myself, and we were totally secure by 3:30. 

So, no, my decision-making is as solid as it was twenty years ago. The hardware up here in my head—the processor, if you will—is running at optimal speed. It's just that power supply issue I keep coming back to. The physical exhaustion. But the actual thinking? The logic and the focus? No problems there whatsoever. I can still out-think anyone in my department on any given day.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant change in psychomotor activity (either agitation or retardation) nearly every day, as this is a key diagnostic criterion that has not been clearly endorsed yet.
doctor.question: Have you noticed that you’ve been moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or that you’ve been unusually restless or unable to sit still, nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor agitation or retardation, which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Moving slowly or... being restless? No, I wouldn't say so. Not at all, really. 

I mean, I'm sixty-three, so I'm not exactly running the hundred-meter dash like I did back in my high school track days, but I get around the office at the exact same pace I always have. If there's a physical hardware issue down in the server room on the second floor, I'm down the stairs and in the racks just as quick as anyone else. And as for speaking slowly... well, you're listening to me right now. I think I keep a pretty standard cadence. If anything, when I'm explaining a complex network topology to the new hires, I actually have to consciously slow myself down, because they just don't grasp the legacy architecture we're running and I end up losing them if I talk at my normal speed. 

And as for being restless, or not being able to sit still... well, I think I just mentioned a minute ago how I sat at my desk for four or five hours straight working on that SQL database issue without even getting up for coffee. You absolutely cannot do that if you're fidgeting or bouncing your leg or needing to pace the halls. I see some of these young guys, these new junior developers, they come in with their giant energy drinks, and they're tapping their pens, shaking their knees under the desk, constantly getting up to pace around or play ping-pong in the breakroom... I honestly don't know how they get a single line of clean code written with all that nervous energy. 

But me? No, I plant myself in my desk chair—Mary actually bought me this fantastic Herman Miller chair for our anniversary a few years back because the standard issue office chairs were doing a number on my lower back, and let me tell you, it was the best investment we ever made—and I just sit there and work. I don't pace, I don't fidget. I just sit and process the data. So, no, none of that physical slowing down or jittery stuff. I'm physically steady. It's really just that battery drain I keep coming back to.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a persistent low mood and loss of interest for at least two years, which would support a diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder (F33.9) over recurrent major depressive disorder (F33.1).
doctor.question: Would you say that your current low mood and loss of interest in activities have been present for most of the day, more days than not, for the past two years without a significant break?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since I was pulled back into full operational leadership, about two years and four months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timeline of the symptoms, specifically whether they have been present for the past two years, which directly corresponds to the duration of the condition.

patient.answer:
Well, let me think about that timeframe. Two years... Actually, if I’m being completely precise—and you know how I am with tracking the details—it’s been a bit longer than that. I’d put it right at about two years and four months. 

I know that specifically because, well, that’s exactly when they pulled me back into full operational leadership at the company. See, before that, I had sort of transitioned into more of an advisory role. A senior systems architect position where I was mostly just consulting on the big-picture infrastructure, you know, handing off the day-to-day firefighting to the younger guys so I could coast a bit toward retirement. Mary and I were even looking at buying an RV, mapping out some national parks we wanted to see. 

But then, of course, our director of IT operations decides to jump ship to some fintech startup out in Silicon Valley, and he leaves us completely high and dry right in the middle of a massive, multi-phase server migration. It was total chaos. The executives were panicking. So, management comes to me, practically begging, saying they need someone with institutional knowledge to steer the ship, and before I know it, I’m back in the trenches. Full operational leadership, managing a team of thirty people, dealing with the daily grind all over again. 

And ever since that happened—which, like I said, was exactly two years and four months ago—it’s just been this constant, low-grade... drag. Every single day. Most of the day, really. I wake up with it, like I mentioned with those early morning wake-ups at four AM, and I just carry it with me through the whole shift, and then I drag it back home with me. There really hasn't been a break from it. Not a real one, anyway. Even when Mary and I took a long weekend up to the lake cabin last fall, which was supposed to be a total disconnect, no laptops allowed, I was still just sitting out on the porch feeling completely flat. Just drained of any actual enthusiasm for being there, or for doing much of anything, really. 

So, yes, to answer your question, it’s been more days than not, pretty much all day, without any real interruption, ever since I got pulled back into that role two years and four months ago.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms have been present for over two years without significant remission, meeting criteria for persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia). No additional disorders were identified based on the information obtained in this turn.
